text.p: Romania issued a new high value banknote on Wednesday -- worth the equivalent of just over $10 -- but it was nowhere to be found on Bucharest streets.
The 50,000 lei banknote, depicting the country's most famous composer George Enescu, was intended to rid Romanians of the problem of having to accumulate large wads of bills to complete transactions.
But a check of shops failed to turn up a single one of the red notes, which feature on their reverse side an Enescu score and a sphynx-like rock formation in the Carpathian mountains.
"I haven't yet seen this banknote, but for me it only means mushrooming inflation," said Tudor Liviu, an unemployed man.
Customers continued to pay for goods in 10,000 lei notes (about $2), supplemented by badly worn smaller denominations.

The leu has been in free fall for a month at currency shops but recovered after last weekend's presidential election victory by reformist Emil Constantinescu and was trading at about 4,600 to the dollar on Wednesday.

Romanians remember times before the 1989 anti-communist revolution when a few thousand lei were enough for a two-week holiday. That sum is now the price of a sandwich and typical salaries are worth around $100.
"This banknote makes me glad because I no longer have to watch the cashier counting my salary in 1,000-lei banknotes," said Cristian Stefanescu, 28.
